explanation: Two of its words are spelled oddly on purpose: Alfa, because some speakers would not read 'ph' as f, and Juliett, so French speakers sound the final t.

claims.text: In the NATO (ICAO radiotelephony) spelling alphabet, the code word for the letter X is X-ray, written Xray in some versions.
Xylophone, Xenon and Xanthippe are not the NATO code word for X; Xanthippe was the X word of an older international alphabet of the 1920s.
The NATO alphabet spells Alfa without 'ph' because speakers unfamiliar with English spelling might not pronounce 'ph' as f.
The NATO alphabet spells Juliett with a double t so that French speakers do not treat a single final t as silent.
The prescribed spellings Alfa and Juliett are deliberate, not errors.

evidence.restatement: The ICAO/ITU radiotelephony alphabet that NATO uses gives X-ray as the word for X; ICAO prints it as Xray in some documents, hyphenated in others.

claimResults.note: Solved cold with high confidence. The full alphabet (Alfa, Bravo ... X-ray, Yankee, Zulu) is standard reference material and unchanged since 1956. Standard risk, so knowledge at certain confidence confirms it.

evidence.restatement: None of Xylophone, Xenon or Xanthippe is the X code word today; Xanthippe (spelled Xantippe in some 1927 lists) was the X word of the CCIR/ITU city-based alphabet of 1927, kept in the 1932 revision.

evidence.summaryExcerpt: The ITU's predecessor, the CCIR, produced the first internationally recognized spelling alphabet. NATO's history page says the list was built mostly from city and country names, and it includes Amsterdam, Baltimore, and Xantippe (NATO spells the X entry "Xantippe" in 1927 and "Xanthippe" in 1932).

claimResults.note: The wrongness of all three distractors is certain: the modern X word is X-ray. The dated aside (date risk) was checked by search: the summary attributes the 1927 CCIR list, with the X entry Xantippe in 1927 and Xanthippe in its 1932 revision, to NATO's own history page (Tier A). So an international alphabet of the 1920s did use this name for X, give or take one letter of spelling, and 'of the 1920s' holds. Only the claim mentions it; the player-facing text does not, so the spelling variant is harmless.

evidence.restatement: ICAO chose the spelling Alfa because readers of languages other than English might not know that the letters p-h together sound like f.

claimResults.note: This is the reason ICAO and NATO give for the non-English spelling, and it is repeated in every standard account of the alphabet (Alfa and Juliett are the two words NATO and ICAO spell this way on purpose). I hold it at certain confidence; under memo 18 this high-risk etymology claim counts if pass B confirms it directly too. No search spent: the batch cap is 2 and this is settled reference material.

evidence.restatement: Juliett carries two t's because a French reader would otherwise drop the sound of a lone t at the end of the word.

claimResults.note: Same standard account as c3: the doubled t exists so that French speakers pronounce the final consonant. Certain from reference knowledge; relies on memo 18 (A and B direct confirmations) for the high-risk label.

evidence.restatement: The official ICAO tables print Alfa and Juliett with those spellings by design; they are the prescribed forms rather than misprints.

claimResults.note: Follows from c3 and c4; the ICAO Annex 10 table uses exactly these forms.

evidence.restatement: The ICAO spelling alphabet that NATO also uses gives X-ray (printed Xray in the official ICAO list) for the letter X.

claimResults.note: Rival test: no other word is used for X in the current alphabet, and the hyphen versus Xray spelling difference does not change the answer. The search result summary also said NATO changed X-ray to Xray, which is the same word.

evidence.restatement: Xenon and Xylophone appear in no official spelling alphabet. The ITU list of 1927 (Amsterdam, Baltimore, Casablanca ... Yokohama, Zurich) did use Xanthippe for X, which is why it is a believable but wrong option.

claimResults.note: Attacked each distractor as a possible second answer: all three are wrong for the present alphabet, so there is no rival key. Xylophone is the classic alphabet-book X word, so it tempts. I searched once and the result neither mentioned Xanthippe nor contradicted it, so the Xanthippe date detail rests on my knowledge only and needs check A's external evidence (high risk).

evidence.restatement: Alfa is written with an f instead of ph so that speakers who do not know English spelling will say the f sound.
